utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. Could we have the appearances for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. Good morning, Counsel. For the Prosecution, Tecla Benjamin, Ekkehard Withopf, and Ruth Karper, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. And could we have the appearances for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel, Stefane Bourgon, co-counsel, and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone in the courtroom that is present for this hearing. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Withopf and Ms. Benjamin, the Defence, the accused, and everyone else present in the courtroom. And I wouldn't want to forget the security officers either. We have two witnesses scheduled for today, according to the document that we have been forwarded. It seems that protective measures will be requested for one of the witnesses. I don't know if this concerns the first witness or the second one. Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, both witnesses are available, as indicated in our recent witness schedule. The first witness scheduled for today requests protective measures, and if we could go, for that purpose, for the application, into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm going to ask you once again to tell us your full name, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Mirko Ivkic. I was born on the 19th of August, 1963, in Blazevac, in Northern Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is your occupation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My occupation, I'm a Catholic priest and an official.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1993, what was your position at the time?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was a priest at the time too, serving in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. You need to take the solemn declaration by reading the text that Madam Usher is going to give you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please be seated. Before giving you some clarifications regarding the proceedings, I wish to ask you first whether you have ever testified in court, or is this the first time for you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time for me to be testifying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As you are testifying for the first time in a court of law, you will have to answer questions which will be put to you by representatives of the Prosecution, who are to your right. The questions will have to do with your position at the time and with the things you yourself saw or heard. At the end of this examination, which will take a certain period of time, the lawyers of one of the accused, who are to your left and who are in the first row, will also ask you some questions within the Anglo-Saxon procedure known as the cross-examination. The three Judges in front of you may, at any point in time, regardless of the questions put to you by the parties, also ask you certain things for the sake of clarification. If a question appears complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it in simple and more understandable terms. Sometimes questions may consist of several questions put in one, and it may be difficult to answer them with precision. When you find yourself in that situation, ask the person asking the question to rephrase it. Also, I need to remind you of some things that you are not aware of but you have to know. You have taken the solemn declaration, which of course means that you may not lie, and lies, in a court of law, are sanctioned by what is known as prosecution by perjury. In the rules that govern our work, which will not apply to you but which I have to recall, is the fact that if, in answering a question, there may be certain incriminating elements, the witness may refuse to answer such a question. The Chamber may compel the witness to answer them, nevertheless, and then the information provided cannot be used as evidence against the witness. Those would be, in very general terms, some points of information regarding the procedure that will be applied during this hearing and your testimony. Without further ado, I turn to Mr. Withopf to start his examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Witness, have you ever studied at a university?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you have studied and where you studied.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I studied in Sarajevo, at the faculty of theology, the philosophy and theology department.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please also inform the Trial Chamber when you studied theology and when you graduated.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I studied from 1983 until 1989, and I graduated that year in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, after you graduated at the University of Sarajevo, what did you do afterwards?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: After that, as an ordained priest, I was ordained after graduation. The ordainment took place on the 29th of June, 1989. And in the autumn of the same year, I was sent to serve as a priest, as a chaplain, in Travnik. A chaplain is the assistant of the main priest in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And for how long, Witness, for how long did you stay in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I stayed in Travnik from the early autumn of 1989 until I left Travnik, which was in mid-June 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you been in Travnik throughout 1989 until June 1993?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And have you been, throughout this period of time, a chaplain?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Up until 1993, in the course of 1993, I acquired responsibility for the whole parish, because the colleague whose assistant I was, was rather ill and virtually I took charge of most things even before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you, Witness, please inform the Trial Chamber in which church, in which Catholic church in Travnik you worked.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: It is the church dedicated to St. John the Baptist. It is in the centre of town, in the street called Titova 97.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This church of St. John Baptist, did it also have a second name, another name?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: It was known as the Church of St. Ivo, or the Lukacka Church.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, have you ever been a member of the Yugoslav People's Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. Army, the JNA?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would you please inform the Trial Chamber from when to when.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Before I enrolled at the university, which means in 1982 to 1983. I don't know exactly. I think up until September of 1983. And immediately after completing my military service, I enrolled at the theology faculty in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: In the first half of 1993, Witness, to your knowledge, which military units were based in the town of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: In the first half of 1993, the military forces that were there were of the HVO, that is, of the Croatian people, and forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, which were, in fact, considered to be Muslim forces in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: The military units of the ABiH, to your knowledge, where were they based in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: To the best of my knowledge, they were stationed in the Marshal Tito Barracks, and I'm not familiar with the structure, nor the actual administration of the army, but the soldiers were there. That is as much as I know. I also know that many soldiers were also at home, and they served by going to the lines and returning home. That applies to the Croats, at least.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Coming back to the ABiH unit in the barracks in Travnik: Do you know which name this unit had or how they were called?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: People referred to the military forces in the Marshal Tito Barracks as the Krajisnici, saying that they had moved in there. They called them the Krajisnici. In fact, however, what this meant was that they had arrived from the outside. As for the local Muslim forces, I can't really say where they were and what units they formed and what different formations existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, Witness: What do you understand by saying "they arrived from the outside"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: This means that those military forces consisted of people who had been expelled, who were refugees, and the name itself tells you where they were expelled from, that is, from Krajina. That is the areas around Banja Luka, Sanski Most, where the Serbian Krajina had been established, and people were simply expelled from there. Many of them were also expelled from the eastern part of Bosnia-Herzegovina. Especially it was not clear who was active in town after the fall of Jajce, which is the larger town in the vicinity of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Witness, can you please tell us who was the commander of the ABiH unit based in the barracks in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, the commander was Mehmed Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did he have a deputy or an assistant?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Another person I knew and whom I considered to be his assistant, and others told me that too, was Cuskic. I don't know what his status was. I think he was a major or something like that, but I am not quite sure about that. I don't know those things. But I know that they were together and that the two of them, in fact, were in charge of the Krajina Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when you noticed foreigners arriving in Travnik or in the area of Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please inform the Trial Chamber, Witness, as to when, for the first time, you noticed such foreigners arriving in Travnik or the area of Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: It was noticeable at the beginning of 1993, especially in March and April. So mostly in the spring of that year.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Have you yourself, Witness, have you yourself seen such foreigners in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, where did these foreigners come from?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: To my knowledge, they were not visitors of Croatian people and Croatian families. They came to visit the Muslims, the local Muslims in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, where did they come from? From which countries?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Among my people, they believed and said that they had come from Islamic countries, such as Afghanistan, Iran, Sudan.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These people from the countries you just mentioned, did they wear any uniforms?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: It was a kind of combination. There were parts that were military uniforms, and also parts of Islamic gear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And were these people armed? Did they have any weaponry?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: They were. Some of them, not all of them, carried the conventional type of weapon. Sometimes they walked around unarmed, sometimes armed. And they also carried weapons that are not meant for war, for parades, various types of knives or swords or something like that, something that was meant to impress that they were there, to make their presence felt. They didn't look like non-combatants.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, can you please explain what you do understand under "conventional type of weapon."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I imply a rifle, a pistol, or things a bit larger than a rifle.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And what things are a bit larger than a rifle?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'm afraid I'm not very qualified to speak about these things, but there are larger rifles that I don't consider to be normal rifles. I don't really know how to put it. I can't go into describing weaponry, because I'm not very well versed in these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you were just stating that they were carrying knives, swords, something that was meant to impress that they were there, to make their presence felt. Were they, to your knowledge, successful in doing so?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: They were. Our people, they didn't carry cameras or tourist maps or anything like that, but they were there to intimidate others, and that is what I heard often from my people, that their presence was not -- did not herald peace.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Just for clarification, Witness: If you are saying you heard it often from your people, are you referring to knowledge you received being a priest in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes. I mean the information and comments regarding what I saw and what others saw. I couldn't see everything, but I saw some very clear signs and very clear -- clearly I saw them parading in town, and I also heard additional comments from others that were made always with a feeling of apprehension and fear regarding their presence in town. Their presence was particularly prominent in the area around the mosque, around the multicoloured mosque. This is the information that I was told.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Being a priest, Witness, did you have a lot of contact to the local people in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. This was not due to any particular efforts on my part, but it was the fact that the people in that area have a great deal of confidence in their priest. They trust him and have hopes from him, and they attach great importance to the opinion of the priest, and that is why they brought this information to me and addressed questions to me as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were saying, Witness, that, and I quote, "Our people were talking to you about the Mujahedin." To what people are you referring to? What do you consider as being "our people"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to my collaborators in the parish where I was active, and also to all the other people who had come to the parish who were members of the parish community. They would come for Sunday mass and for masses celebrated on other days. I could feel their fear too.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And of what ethnicity, Witness, were the members of your parish community?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: They were of Croatian nationality.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did these armed people, foreign armed people, with different kinds Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of uniforms, were they referred to using a certain name, a certain expression?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: They were immediately called the Mujahedin. No other term was used to refer to them. That was the main name used when describing them.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And these armed Mujahedin in different kind of uniforms, to your knowledge and from what you've seen, did they appear as single persons in Travnik or in bigger groups?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I didn't see big groups, but I would see small groups or groups of two. They were in certain areas. They would move around the area. Their presence was quite obvious, because they stood out. They didn't look like the other people that you would see in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For the benefit of the Trial Chamber, Witness, can you please explain why they stood out.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The clothes they wore stood out, the colour of their skin, their complexion, their hair. These things stood out. And although a large part of the population of the town was Muslim, they looked different from both communities. They also wore headbands at times, or something around their necks. I can't describe this very precisely, but they were very obvious. They could be spotted very easily, both by the Muslims, the local Muslims, and by the local Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: These armed Mujahedin, did they have a collection point in Travnik or a certain area where they gathered?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I believe that the witness has already answered this question. The witness said that it was near the Sarena Dzamija, the Sarena mosque.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that that was the area that they would often move around. Large numbers would often gather there. As to where they gathered, where they had their headquarters, where they organised themselves, I am not in a position to tell you much about this. I know nothing about this. But their presence in the town was quite evident and they were frequently seen there. In fact, it amounted to mystifying the people who were present there, in the sense that they wanted to instil fear among the Croats, the Catholic population present in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, in June 1993, was there still the HVO in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: In June 1993, the HVO was no longer present in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: To your knowledge, when had the HVO units, when have the HVO units withdrawn from Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you when precisely, but given the religious holidays, I know that it was around Easter. It was in spring. I don't know whether it was at the end of March or at the beginning of April. I really don't know the exact dates, and I didn't pay attention to this at the time because I had a lot of duties to perform. We were under a lot of psychological pressure and we had a lot of work to do, as there were a lot of refugees in the town, and I worked in Caritas. I was responsible for providing refugees in Travnik with assistance, with aid.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Whilst working for the Caritas, and in this context, did you ever have contact to ABiH soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: No. I had almost no contact whatsoever with the army, up until the time when the conflict escalated, and then, after the conflict escalated, I had a lot of contact with them. Then there were situations. They would enter houses and so on. I can't say which formations were concerned, and I can't tell you how authority, and especially military authority, was established in the area of Travnik. I know that the military conflict between the Croats and the Muslims placed us at risk in our house in the centre of town. We had contact with them, not because we wished to have such contact but because they would appear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did you, Witness, in your position, or working for the Caritas, did you ever provide ABiH soldiers with any food or other supplies?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Before that conflict broke out, cooperation with the Muslim charitable organisations was initially good. We had good cooperation with them. We helped some of the Muslims too. And I assume that Muslim charities also helped our people. But the food that I had at my disposal was never provided to the army. But once the conflict had escalated, then some of the food that was in the basement of the house was quite simply confiscated. And when I asked for it, when I said that I was responsible for those goods, for the food intended for the people, they said that they would make a note of this. Finally, I signed something, to the effect that this was a gift I was giving to the BH army. At that point, a lorry arrived in front of the house and they collected everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And, Witness, was it actually a gift you've given to the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: That's what I had to sign. I didn't give the army a gift of any kind. I didn't give the army anything. So it was a gift, in inverted commas.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Does it mean that you were forced by the ABiH to provide them with food that was meant by Caritas to be given to the people in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I was forced to sign this document, but I couldn't prevent them from taking these goods from the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And if you are saying you couldn't prevent them from taking these goods from the house, whom are you making reference to, if you say "them"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the BH army, the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time, Witness, when you've given a statement on the local radio in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And can you please tell the Trial Chamber as to when you've given such a statement on the local radio in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I made those statements in the course of intense fighting, after the conflict between the BH army and the HVO had escalated. As I was in the town and was not able to establish contact with refugees or with the other part of my people, I was quite simply forced to remain in Travnik. I was forced to remain in my house. And I had the opportunity of making a statement on the radio. When I say that I had the opportunity of making such a statement, that doesn't mean that I actually wanted to take advantage of that opportunity.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what the statement was about.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I spoke about the very beginning about the time when the majority of the Croatian population was expelled from the surrounding villages and from the area of Travnik, from the town itself, and mostly from the outskirts of the town, because they were in a position to flee two, three, four, five days later. I can't be very precise. So it's on that occasion that I made a statement, and I also made a statement after the church in Travnik had been damaged. I remember that I did this on two occasions.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you just said: "When I say that I had the opportunity of making such a statement, that doesn't mean that I actually wanted to take advantage of that opportunity." Can you please, in more detail, inform the Trial Chamber what that means.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Well, when I said that, I meant that I couldn't speak freely on Radio Travnik, and my statements depended on the situation I was in and on the situation that the other inhabitants of Travnik were in. This influenced what I actually said. I wanted something to be done to avoid having a large number of victims, to prevent -- to ensure that civilians were not killed. Because the population spent months in fear, especially when the HVO withdrew from Travnik. The tension was rising at the time. Things had come to a head, and I wanted to take action. I wanted to do something. I wanted the information to get through. However, the information I wanted to provide couldn't be provided. This was simply not possible. So when I had the opportunity of speaking on the radio, I took this to be an opportunity to cooperate, in inverted commas, and this would be to the benefit of the Muslims. This would help the BH army in achieving their objectives.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Based on what you just told us, Witness, cooperation, in inverted commas, does that mean you did not volunteer to say what you actually said on the radio? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The first time I spoke, I asked for any sort of access to the media. This was made possible only after they already knew what my position was and what my assessment of the situation was. And then I was supported in doing this. And the dramatic events -- I was supported in my effort to diminish the seriousness of the events, and I saw that I was no longer in a position to go back. And then what I said was what the Muslims expected me to say. It was what they had suggested I should say. Otherwise, I wouldn't have had access to the media. In fact, when I did gain access to the media, this was very perfidious. I had almost no contact with the Croats at the point. I only had contact with the Muslims, or the Muslim army and their authorities. My activity was reduced to nothing. Although many people were killed, I wasn't able to move around freely. I wasn't able to leave my house, except when there were statements of this kind that I had to make.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, can you please inform the Trial Chamber what was the gist of the statements you made on the radio in Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: When I first spoke on the radio, what I said, essentially, amounted to justifying the Muslim people -- not the Muslim people; the Muslims, the Muslim forces - I apologise - who had entered a conflict with the Croats. I was to show that they were innocent, and I was to accuse the Croatian leadership and declare them to have instigated the conflict. I was to appeal to the Croats to return. But this was only after they had already left, because that is an important factor. The Croatian people, after the escalation occurred, were between Travnik, down below, and the Serbian positions which were further up. There were a lot of people there, several thousand, as far as I know, and they set off in the direction of the other side. So they couldn't return. And the second time I spoke on the radio, I was supposed to speak about the positive situation in Travnik, in inverted commas, the very positive situation. And with regard to the destruction of the church and of all the sacred objects in the church, I was supposed to show that the destruction, the damage, wasn't extensive. I was supposed to describe it as an accidental act of no great importance. The second time I spoke on the radio, I was summoned to do so. I had no choice. I had to make such a statement on the radio. I was forced to go to the radio. I wasn't allowed to leave the house any more, but I was forced to go and make this statement. I also wanted to hear me read out what I heard written down first. I read this out over the telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I just stop you here, Witness, in order to ask you a few follow-up questions. You were informing the Trial Chamber that you made twice statements on the radio. Do you recall, even if it's on roughly, the dates as to when you made such statements you just described?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The first time was at the very beginning of the escalation. I couldn't tell you the exact day, because I was in a very bad state at the time, just like everyone else who had remained in Travnik, so I didn't make a note of the day, of the date. I know it was at the beginning of June, the 2nd or the 3rd or the 4th perhaps. I left Travnik before the day when the parish celebrates its patron saint. That was the 24th of June. So it was during that period that I and the others in Travnik went through terrible things, and it was during that period that I appeared on the radio on those two occasions, once at the beginning, and the second time, after the 7th of June, if I'm not mistaken. That's after the church had been damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And we are talking about June 1993, don't we [sic]?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you were just mentioning that your house was guarded during this period of time. Who actually guarded your house?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: There was no one around the house at the beginning, but various troops or groups of troops would enter the house. They searched for weapons. They took the car. During the night, there was a lot of disturbance. They also opened fire on the house after a certain period of time. We were assigned two BH army soldiers. That's what I assume. I know one of them very well. He was a nice young man. I knew the other person too. They moved into the house, into the lower part of the house, and they were there as guards, in order to protect us, in order to guard us.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: One last question prior to the break, with the permission of the Trial Chamber. Witness, who was searching your house for weapons, and who took the car?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Various formations or groups of soldiers. They were wearing military uniforms. That was a time of war. They were carrying weapons and wearing military uniforms. They would enter the house. And on one occasion - I've also mentioned this in my statement - on one occasion they entered the house at the very beginning, because a commander of a group or of a police force asked me to contact the Croatian side and to ask Mr. Leutar, the HVO commander -- his children and wife were there and I was told to ensure that nothing would happen to them. I did this gladly. I phoned them. And we were insulted, threatened. We were wondering what would happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, if we could now make the break, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to have the break now. It is 10.30. And we will resume at five to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf, you may continue your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, how did the Croatian population in Travnik receive your statements made on the radio, did you get to know about?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I learnt, when I left and went to Novi Travnik, that they were simply disappointed, and there was a division of view. Some thought that it was madness, what I had said, and others, who thought better of it, knew why I had said that. And as they realised how dramatic the conditions were down there, they were less surprised by what I had said. In any event, my first statement on the radio was shocking for Croats, who were the victims and who had to listen to such a statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, can you please, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, describe the situation of Croats in Travnik in May and June 1993. Were they allowed to leave the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: In May, it was still possible to freely leave and enter the town, though at the entrance to the town, especially the area towards Novi Travnik, there were frequently checkpoints established there, near the Sarena Dzamija, the multicoloured mosque, I was stopped on a couple of occasions, and again close to Plava Voda, along that route. Maybe I didn't quite understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Did there come a time -- did there come a time, Witness, just to clarify this, when you asked for permission to leave Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: May I just add to my answer to the previous question. One could come and go until the conflict escalated. When the town was hermetically closed, no one could leave or come in. And with time, I realised that the people were in grave danger, who wanted to leave and couldn't leave. I too wanted to leave at all cost, because, as time passed, I felt I was in danger and at great personal risk. And in view of my position and the role I had in Travnik before that, and the fact that I had stayed in the town, the only person visible in the parish office who could represent the Croatian people in Travnik was myself, but I was unable to perform that duty in the interest of the Croats, but I was used as an instrument, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you were just saying that the town was hermetically closed. Who was actually closing the town?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The military activities caused this, so that I can't tell you exactly who it was who ordered it, or under what conditions it was sealed. I just know that it was impossible to leave, because there was a lot of Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. shooting. And when there wasn't any shooting, I didn't have the possibility, nor the right, to leave. This could only be done through the mediation of UNPROFOR or through the mediation of the military forces, in my case, through the forces of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you were just saying that there were many checkpoints. Soldiers of which army did man the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: On the town side were the soldiers of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Let's move on, Witness, to a different issue. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber where the house you were living in at the time, where in Travnik it is and was located.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The house I was living in was located in the centre of town, next to the church, which is also in the centre of town, in Titova Street, which was a pedestrian area.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when the church in Travnik, when the church was negatively affected by the conflict?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes. The church was affected by the conflict. If you mean the building itself, the church as a building was the target of fire, with firearms. But the most dramatic incident occurred when the church was broken into and totally demolished.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when it happened, even if you only do know a rough date.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: This happened in the early part of the month of June. I think it was on the 7th. I don't know what day of the week it was. In the morning. All we could do was to stay in the house, and we couldn't go out. And then on the 7th of July [as interpreted], the church was broken into, and the demolition of the inside started. There were loud noises of destruction inside the church itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I please, Witness, may I please interrupt you for a second to clarify an issue. The transcript says on the 7th of July. Was it the 7th of July or the 7th of June?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: No, no. It can't be July. That's an error. I'm sorry. In July I was no longer in Travnik. I must also tell you that the names of the month, even I don't use the Croatian names; I most often use the regular names: January, February, March. So I may make a slip of the tongue. But anyway, I meant the beginning of the sixth month, which is June.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness, for the clarification. Can you please, in detail, describe, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, what happened at the day the interior of the church, as you already said, was demolished.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: In the morning, I was sleeping, and I fell asleep out of exhaustion, because there was shooting until late into the night and there were provocations around the house and there was shooting into the house, into the interior, into the rooms. And we never knew when the house would really be broken into and what would happen to us. In any event, we were living in a great deal of fear and uncertainty. That morning, we heard a lot of noise, and the lady who lived in the house with us heard it. She was a person who was temporarily working in the house. She was like a sort of cook. And also, a priest, my older colleague, who had been my superior up to a couple of months prior to that, but he stayed with me because he too couldn't leave Travnik. And when she woke me up, I jumped up immediately because I heard clearly that something terrible was happening in the church, and because of all the fear that had accumulated, in my mind, I knew that demolishing the church could just be the beginning of the fury of destruction. So that I expected the possibility of them breaking into the house, but there weren't so many sacral objects in the house for destruction. But we, as human beings, were aware of the danger we were in. So that I started dialling various numbers, in panic, hoping that someone would react and come and see what was going on and take control of the situation and stop it. I called up many numbers of the civilian and military authorities, that is, the Muslim authorities, people who were in charge of the town and who were responsible for the town, who had the town under control and who had occupied the town and held it and sealed it. Those moments seemed like eternity, because no one would come, and time was flying. Though some would console me by saying they would come, others said that they couldn't control these things because there was a lot of chaos in town. The people I did call, among others, was the barracks of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I don't know who was at the other end of the line. I cannot be specific about those structures. I can't call them by their names because I'm not familiar with their competencies and the responsible groups. But I dialled a lot of numbers, including Plava Voda and the police in the main street. About 200 or 300 metres from my own house, I also called up some friends. I called up a Muslim, a doctor, Izet Kreho, and he promised that he would call back. And out of panic and fear I begged him to do something, that it may be a question of minutes before they would break into the house. And I also told him that they were Mujahedins who were doing this.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, may I just interrupt you here for a second. You just informed the Trial Chamber that you, amongst other people, called the ABiH barracks in Travnik. To your recollection, what did you tell them at this point in time?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: To my recollection, I told them what was most important, that they should prevent the destruction of the church, that we were in danger. I spoke of the demolition of the church, that it was being destroyed mercilessly. And I appealed to them. I begged them to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what happened after your phone calls.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: My phone calls took place while I was watching what was going on outside, because the church was just in front of the house. So it is possible to see the entrance to the church from the upper floor. So I had a good view of what was going on in front of the church, and I saw that this was continuing. And so I combined my activities on the phone with thoughts as to an escape route. But I called up people again, because that is all I could do during that time of agony.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For how long, Witness, did what you described as the demolishing of the interior of the church, for how long did it go on?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: According to my judgement, and the situation was quite exceptional, in view of what was going on, this went on from about 7.00, or just after 7.00, or just before 7.00, until about 8.30, maybe even up to 9.00. In my judgement, this went on for about an hour and a half or two. And the two soldiers who were in the lower part of the house, who were sleeping in the office premises, I cautioned them of what was going on and I asked them again: "Have you done anything? Do something." However, they first tried to do something, and then one soldier said to me: "They're crazy. We are afraid too." And they locked themselves in, inside. When you enter the house, to the right, there was another door, and they locked themselves in. Because one soldier said that he -- when he went to caution this person, he didn't understand him. He said they were Mujahedins and he kicked him in the stomach and pointed his gun at him. One Mujahedin was keeping guard in front of the church which was being demolished inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You just mentioned earlier on that your house was close to the church and that you could hear and see clearly. Can you please tell the Trial Chamber what you have heard between 7.00 and about 9.00 on that day.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I heard some very loud noise, banging and breaking things. That is all that I could hear. Because it was the morning, and usually it was quite quiet in the morning. There were no military activities going on in the distance that one could hear. Also, it was a sunny day, so the view was absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And whilst you heard, between 7.00 and about 9.00, whilst you heard what was going on inside the church, did anybody come to help you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I was horrified to see that it was not possible to get anyone to come, although it was so nearby. We felt helpless. And when the job had been completed, our fear peaked, and when a soldier headed towards the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. house, someone appears to have reacted, because I know that there was a brief but very loud argument, and the Mujahedin who were in the church, thank God, were not allowed to enter the house. After that, when I saw that they wanted to enter the house as well, I didn't really follow, but I realised that they wanted to enter the house, because one of the soldiers who had gone to caution the soldier in front of the church also locked the whole house. And the lady who was in the house was completely distraught. She was hysterical. But now that I look back at those reactions, I know that she said to me that we should flee towards the roof, towards the attic, go to the attic. And then she cried out: "They're going to slit the throat of Vinko," who was my sick colleague, and he was on the first floor, in the private premises. He was in a room, lying exhausted and very sick. And then when I was told that the soldiers had left, one of the people who had stopped them was there, and then I too went downstairs. I greeted those present. We spoke for a while in front of the house and then we entered the house.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: May I just interrupt you here, Witness. You just said -- you made reference, "When the job had been completed." Can you please inform the Trial Chamber what you mean by saying, "The job had been completed."

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: What I mean is when the church was totally demolished inside, the interior of the church, because I was able to see that for myself afterwards. There wasn't a single object that had not been damaged. And in a church such as the Travnik church, there were many, many objects, because, by its position and its age, it had some important valuables. There was an organ, there were sculptures, there were paintings, there were glass windows, and not a single one was left intact. Then there was the internal door, which was also partly in -- glazed. Then the loudspeaker system. Everything, literally everything, was destroyed. The tabernacle, the most important part of a church, was also broken, and sacral objects had been damaged and indented.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, can you please inform the Trial Chamber as to when you've seen this damage you've just described?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I saw the damage after talking to the people who had come to prevent and to see what was going on. These were representatives of the town authorities. These are my assumptions, because, actually, I called up anyone had any position in town to try and prevent it and assist. Now, who actually appeared among all those I called, I can't really say, but I do believe that they were representatives of the town, also representatives of the [indiscernible], and representatives of the Krajisnici, that is, the soldiers in the barracks. They would come in twos and immediately they went inside, and the conversation lasted about half an hour to 45 minutes, and then I too went into the church. Before that, the lady who was with us, she had the courage to go and see immediately. Because while I was talking to them, I asked: "What happened over there?" She just waved her hand, and I can't repeat her words, but she said something to the effect that it was as if the devil himself had entered and destroyed everything inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you were earlier on mentioning the damage to the organ. Can you please go into some detail in that respect.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The organ, in my assessment, I just couldn't believe that such damage could be done so quickly, because to destroy an organ, I thought would take more time. I couldn't analyse it, because I left Travnik a couple of days or maybe a week later. So I could simply cast a glance at the organ, and I was astonished that all the organ parts had been indented, broken, and the damage was quite considerable to look at. It was a catastrophe regarding the organ. But there was so much damage that one could hardly walk.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You also mentioned that sculptures and paintings were damaged. Can you please in some more detail describe the damage to the sculptures and paintings.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Paintings and sculptures were simply destroyed, so that many paintings were -- had holes in them. The sculptures had their heads or arms broken off, or the faces destroyed, so they were unrecognisable and they couldn't be used. As I was looking at things then, I thought that it would -- not a single of those objects could be used again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What about the windows?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The windows were also partly -- I can't remember the details. I just have a memory of the horror. But I can't say whether one or maybe two remained whole. But anyway, the windows were damaged.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, did there come a time when you informed representatives of the ABiH in Travnik about the damage to the church in Travnik you just described?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes. And in view of my position, I couldn't move freely or write or come and go. But a representative of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, representatives of the Krajisnici, came to see me, representatives of the civilian authorities too. And it was so obvious for them that there was no need for me to inform them about it or to see what they thought about it. Their questions were mostly directed to me as to what should be done with me, because the only thing that remained for the Croats in Travnik, where they used to come to before the conflict, had now been destroyed. So there was no chance for me to invite people to come to the church and to hold any kind of service there, especially as I realised immediately that the church had been desecrated and destroyed. So what I wanted to do was to inform the public, or at least for my bishop to be informed, to know that the church had been damaged and the church should again be renovated so as to be able to be used again as a church. So regarding the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Cuskic was present that morning. I know that full well, that he was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And did you talk to Mr. Cuskic, whom you earlier on described today as an assistant to Mr. Alagic, the commander of the Krajisnici? Did you talk to him?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did. We spoke to each other. I don't remember everything that was said. I know that he expressed his dissatisfaction when he asked who had done that. And this was done in the presence of everyone. He was told that it was the Mujahedin. He was told that that was clear, and the troops who were in the house were well aware of this fact. And he reacted in a very emotional way, in a positive way, in relation to the damage done to the building. He said that those people should be removed, that they should be killed, that they should be prevented from doing such things in the town. What he said was sincere, and one could feel that he wasn't satisfied with what had happened. That was my impression. Others didn't seem very sorry about this. I have to say that no one told me, as the parish priest, that they felt regret for what had happened. No one apologised, neither at the time nor in the following few days. And even Cuskic had reacted as he had, didn't say that he was sorry about what had happened. He didn't go into the reasons for why this had happened. I don't know how to describe his reaction, but, on the one hand, the reaction was negative; but on the other hand, I didn't feel that he or the BH army thought that much damage had been done when this act was committed. It didn't seem as if they thought that a lot of evil had been committed. But the civil protection said that they wanted to organise the people, to clean up. And then the lady in our house said that they would do it. She said that she didn't want Muslims to go into the church. She said that they could clean everything up and sort everything out.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, if I just may interrupt you here for a follow-up question. Mr. Cuskic, did he actually see the damage? Was he led inside the church?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I didn't take anyone inside. One could say that they took me inside. I was no longer in the position of a host. I was no longer a sovereign and free man who could freely express his positions, given that he was aware of what had happened and how delicate the situation was. I didn't comment on this, and I really didn't want to express an explicit opinion on the matter. But I do know that Cuskic must have gone in, because the church isn't two kilometres away. It's only ten metres from Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the house. So I can't really know who was in the group, because they would go in and come out. I stayed on in some parts of the church itself and examined the state it was in.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: You were just saying, Witness, that, "They took me inside." Whom are you referring to by saying "they"?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to people who had taken me in. We went in together. It's not as if there was a consensus, an agreement. It's not as if we had agreed to have a look. As we were speaking to each other, some people went in, examined the state. It's not far away. They would comment on what they had seen, and after I had seen the last guests off, after we had gone outside, then I set off in the direction of the church. I don't know exactly who was with me. There was this lady who was already in the church. She had a look at the church. Then she returned to the house again, then went out again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you earlier on informed the Trial Chamber that Mr. Alagic was in charge of the ABiH unit in the Travnik Barracks. Did there come a time, Witness, when you talked to Mr. Alagic about the devastation of the interior of the church?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I had contact with Mr. Alagic in order to obtain permission to leave Travnik. I didn't say that it was a matter of leaving Travnik. I said it was a matter of contacting Croats in Novi Travnik, on the other side. And military action was undertaken on that side too. I continued to insist on this, and I always asked for someone in a position of responsibility who might make this possible for me. I saw that things were becoming even more tense, and on the basis of my experience, I saw that they couldn't make the situation easier for me. My intention was simply to survive and inform others about the situation, because I didn't have any contact with the press, with journalists. I wanted the situation to be examined, but they wanted this to be used for their own objectives. My wishes weren't listened to. I had contact with Alagic in relation to this matter, and the discussions we had related to the church, but he didn't give any importance to what had happened in the church. And Asim Gradincic, my mentor, who monitored my duties, my contacts, when I asked him who could give me permission, who could make this possible for me, he said that only Mr. Alagic was in a position to give me such permission. So I just visited Cuskic and Alagic on one occasion. Alagic didn't comment on the church. Cuskic touched on the matter. If Alagic said anything about it, I don't remember that. But he must have been aware of what had happened. I know that he didn't pay any attention to this at all. He didn't take it into account and he didn't ask me about the situation. I also didn't want to say anything much about it. I knew the matter was very delicate, and I didn't want to tell him what I felt, because I knew they wouldn't like it, and I knew that the issue was very sensitive.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: For clarification, Witness: When, to your recollection, or how many days after the interior of the church was demolished, when did you talk to Mr. Alagic about it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: At that time, during those days or weeks, I was in such a state that I couldn't really tell you about the days or dates when this happened. I know that it was shortly afterwards, but I couldn't say whether it was two or three days later. It's very difficult for me to remember this now.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say, Witness, that it was a matter of days rather than a matter of weeks or months?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: It was certainly after several days. I can state that for certain. It wasn't more than one week later.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Earlier on today, Witness, you were mentioning that you wanted to get your bishop to know about the demolishment of the church in Travnik. Did there come a time when your bishop got to know about it?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I was able to speak to the bishop in the evening, at about 11.00. I was taken to the premises where they had the necessary technical equipment, and the conversation was about what had happened. I informed him about what had happened. I asked him whether he would be in a position to visit Travnik or do something to prevent civilians from being killed in Travnik. I said that the church was no longer a holy building and that it couldn't be used as such. He said that he would visit the Travnik [as interpreted] as soon as possible, given that he was familiar with the situation there. But the date he mentioned was problematic; the date was postponed. On the day he was supposed to come and visit us, the bishopric building in Sarajevo was shelled, which made it impossible for him to come on the day that he had mentioned. He came later, perhaps on the 19th or 20th, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Once -- or when the bishop from Sarajevo came to Travnik, did the bishop speak to anybody from the ABiH?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: He came to the parish flat where I lived. Representatives of the town authorities and of the military authorities appeared there. I was present. A colleague of mine was present who had also been detained in the town, in the monastery. Everyone who was affected by this, everyone who was responsible for the events, everyone who had a role of some kind in the town, appeared. Representatives of the Muslim religious community were also present there.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Which military authorities are you referring to who were present at this meeting?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'm referring to the leaders of Krajina, from -- the troops from the barracks, and I'm also referring to other military formations in the town, perhaps the police as well, and civilian forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Was the issue of the demolishing of the interior of the church in Travnik, was it discussed?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it was. Many events were discussed, and the fact that the civilians were at risk. There was also an exodus from that area. But in addition to these matters, the church was also mentioned, and the cardinal quite clearly condemned this and showed respect for the people who were present there, but he condemned this act of barbarism, and the others present agreed with this assessment. So, on the one hand, the situation was tense, but, on the other, positions were freely expressed, and the act was condemned by both sides, something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, you earlier on today mentioned that you left Travnik. Can you please, very briefly, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber, describe the circumstances under which you left Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: When my bishop visited Travnik, that was the day on which I was released and when I managed to get out of that terrible situation. I took advantage of his presence in the house to speak to him briefly, in person, and I asked him if I could go to Novi Travnik with him. I didn't tell him that I had to leave the entire area. My purpose was simply to move away, move out of the house and to escape from the danger I felt. I told him that it was necessary for me to leave and that if anything was to be done in the field, the other side had to be contacted. He said: "I'm not responsible for this. I can't ask anyone. I can't do anything." But he said: "Come with me, and if it's possible, you'll get into the personnel carrier, and if there's room, you can go with us." I didn't tell him about everything. It wasn't until we got to Novi Travnik that I told him what was at stake, and I'm glad that he didn't ask me about all the details. And in some way, he understood what was at stake, in spite of the fact that he hadn't understood everything. He didn't know that I was in a very difficult situation. And I left Travnik, accompanied by the bishop and his secretary. There were others who were escorting him, representatives from the town, military representatives. I remember going to the vehicle, and a lot of people were standing around. Cuskic was there, and there were some others too. I managed to get through to him, and my intention was to enter the vehicle after he had got in. I wanted to get out of the town, because I felt that the situation was critical, and I thought that if I didn't take advantage of that situation, I wouldn't survive. So I got into the vehicle and I was glad that he hadn't been stopped, because, given all the manipulation, I wasn't able to get away from Travnik, and those in positions of responsibility didn't do anything and didn't try to do anything. Asking them to do something was all to no avail.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, after you left Travnik, did you ever go back to Travnik to serve in the Travnik parish?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Never again.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: What did you do, and if you could please briefly summarise it, after you left Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: When I got out of Travnik, I was in Novi Travnik. That was an enclave. Nova Bila, Vitez, Busovaca. I stayed there until the beginning of November. In November, I think that I managed to get out of that enclave. Up until that time, I was in a place called Rankovici, near Novi Travnik, on the side under Croatian control. My life there was -- well, I was forced to stay there. You couldn't go further on. And while I was there, I helped that colleague of mine, and I also had a lot of contact with my people, because there were a lot of refugees from Travnik who were there on the other side.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: And afterwards, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: When I got out, by helicopter, from Herzegovina, I ended up in Split. From Split, I went to Zagreb. In Split, I visited many refugees from Travnik, friends and acquaintances. They were very happy to see that I had survived. Some of them had been misinformed. I don't know where they had obtained their information from. According to some of the information they had been given, I had lost my mind. Apparently something had happened to me in Travnik, because the situation was so bad. Fortunately, that wasn't true. Later I went to our office for refugees, the bishopric office in Zagreb, and as I had left without any resources, without any possessions, I didn't have any clothes, apart from the ones that I was wearing -- well, in Zagreb, I had the possibility of spending some time in a house that the bishopric had in Zagreb, and if I felt capable of taking charge of one of the refugee centres, I was given this possibility. There were many such centres in Croatia at the time. I accepted such duties in a Croatian refugee centre near Ogulin. I spent two years there. And then I was in Split again. And my duties became normal, in a certain sense. I wasn't involved in my own bishopric, but with the permission of my bishopric, I worked in other bishoprics. I spent one year in Italy, and now I've spent five or six years in Germany.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, to your knowledge, has the damage done to the church in Travnik, has it been repaired?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: My brother, my colleague, who became a priest in 1996 or 1997, he was in Zenica and then in the area of Travnik, where he worked as a priest. When I visited him, I passed through Travnik on a number of occasions. Sometimes I would stay in Novi Travnik for a while, and I would visit people who knew me and who knew what I had been through. Then on one occasion, I went into that church. I looked around. And arriving in that town, it had such an effect on me that I wanted to get away very quickly. What I saw in that church was a pleasant surprise. The colleague who took over after me was quite successful in his attempts to make the building look good on the outside. Some of the sculptures hadn't exactly been repaired, but let's say the patron saint, the head of the patron saint I think had been put back on the sculpture. But it hadn't exactly been replaced. And there were many other things. Certain things -- many things couldn't be repaired because they had been destroyed. So I briefly had a look at the church, and I noticed that what could be repaired had been repaired, for example, ordinary windows, whereas other things, things that were difficult to repair, hadn't been repaired, and I don't think that they've been repaired to this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Witness, how do you feel today about the demolition of the interior of the church, of the Travnik church?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: When I come up close, well, then I feel as if I've been returned to that situation and this brings tears to my eyes. It creates a feeling of helplessness, of humiliation. I become another person. Because this was very painful for me, especially this very insecure situation. The lack of freedom also had a significant effect on me. So if I go back to that time, to what I felt at the time, it's as if you are -- it's as if you are putting someone back into a frying pan and you have this person begging others to release him from this torture. Since 15 years have passed since then, I have created perhaps an internal mechanism which allows me to speak about this without feeling very emotional. But when I have to relive all these experiences, I feel threatened, insecure, and I must say that at the time, I just wanted someone to find out that this had to be prevented. But I just wanted to survive. That was my only objective. I saw what the situation was, it was critical, and luckily, I was able to get out of the town with the bishop. I would just like to add that I don't blame any one person. I don't feel that I need compensation of some kind. I don't feel that there is someone who is responsible as an individual for what happened. I know that this was a result of the war. But I'm simply glad that I managed to survive. At the time, I felt no hatred either, but I was angry. I was angry because nothing could be done, and I was angry because people were humiliated in such a calculating and unscrupulous way.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. Ivkic.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, this concludes the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Withopf. I turn now to Defence counsel to give them the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Ivkic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'm Edina Residovic.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I know that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And I represent General Enver Hadzihasanovic. I will be asking you some questions in connection with your testimony and in connection with the fact that, at the time of the events, you were a respected personality in the town of Travnik. You said that you completed studies of theology in 1989 in Sarajevo and that you became a priest; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, as you told my learned friend from the Prosecution, you were sent to serve in the Travnik bishopric and you started serving in the Church of St. John the Baptist in Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: At the time, and for many years and centuries before that, Travnik was inhabited by a mixture, an ethnically mixed population: Serbs, Croats, and Muslims. But just before the war, the Muslims were in the majority; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, there were more of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Relations between ethnicities and people of different faiths in Travnik were traditionally good?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: In my time, very good.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were born in the village of Blazevac, next to Gradacac, in Bosnia, one could say Northern Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: North-eastern Bosnia, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And where you were born, too, relations between ethnicities and faiths were traditionally good; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a Bosnian priest, you believed that you should do everything in your power for all peoples to remain in their homes and for their church or mosque to be the place where they would gather; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you have already said - and this is something this Trial Chamber is well aware of - in April 1992, immediately after the proclamation of independence, the Yugoslav People's Army attacked Bosnia and the Serb forces; is that true?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The town of Travnik, where you served, was shelled from Mount Vlasic in the first months following the attack on Bosnia; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I think so. I'm afraid I'm not quite sure about the chronology. I can't give you the exact dates where it started first.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, as a citizen of Travnik, you certainly know that Serb forces captured the Komar pass and the tops of Mount Vlasic, and that they had come to a close distance, a dangerous distance, from Travnik. They were halted at Turbe, in fact, which is about 12 kilometres away from Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Already in the course of 1992, several dozen thousand refugees arrived in Travnik, first from Krajina, who had been expelled from there by the Serb forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: A fresh wave of refugees arrived in Travnik at the end of 1992, when the town of Jajce fell to the Serb forces; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The arrival of such large numbers of refugees to Travnik, which was not such a large city, created many problems regarding accommodation and food and relations in the town itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, both the civilian and military authorities, as well as the charitable organisations of the Croatian and Muslim peoples, did everything they could to alleviate the difficulties; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As you stated earlier on, you noticed that there was tension between the two peoples and between members of the HVO and the BH army early in the spring of 1993; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, in that period of time, there were both units of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina in town, as well as units of the HVO; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You said that units of the army, the Krajisnici, as you call them, were quartered in the former barracks in Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: That is my own knowledge and experience.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It may be a slip, but it is a barracks that was called after hero Petar Mecava and not Marshal Tito. Would you agree with me that this may have been a mix-up?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: You may be right. I knew it as the Marshal Tito Barracks, but I am not sure. I may be wrong. Maybe I have been misinformed. I don't know how that name stuck in my mind.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps because we have such a barracks in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Certainly, as an important figure in the life of particularly the Croatian people in Travnik, you know that on the 8th of April there was a large meeting of all leaders of the HDZ and the HVO, of the so-called Herceg-Bosna. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Two days prior to that, reinforced police units of the HVO had arrived in Travnik. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I do not.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This meeting that was also attended by Dario Kordic, as the vice-president of the HVO in Herceg-Bosna, as well as commanders from the whole area, there was a discussion on the expedited implementation of the Vance-Owen Plan, which still hadn't been signed. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: At the time, I didn't have much occasion to analyse the political events. I was extremely active with regard to Caritas activities and the refugees. So I believe what you say, but I cannot comment with any reliability.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you know that on that day, on the 8th of April, Croatian flags were hoisted on important buildings and that, in view of the importance of the meeting and the preparations of a part of the population to celebrate Easter, and another part of the population who was celebrating the 10th of April as the independence day of Croatia, that this was seen as a provocation by a certain section of the population.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I don't know all those things because, simply, I didn't perceive them. I only realised what happened when things happened, and I wondered why.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you knew that something happened, that certain members of the army took down the flags and set fire to them and that the HVO killed two to three soldiers of the BH army? You knew that fact?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This incident actually heightened tensions which had already started increasing between the two ethnic groups in the town of Travnik; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Certainly, but I don't know the circumstances behind that incident, why it occurred and what preceded it and the circumstances around it, so I can't say much about that. I just am aware of the incident because it occurred close to the church.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: After that, the Croatian Defence Council started, by means of propaganda, and in practice, to instigate the population, to encourage them to leave should a conflict break out with the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and you, as a Bosnian priest, could not agree with that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: What you just last said is correct, that, as a priest, I did not have officially, nor personally, as I identified with my people and the church leadership, which advocated full support for people to remain in their homes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That brings me to my next question. A cardinal today, and in those days, the Catholic bishop for Bosnia, Mr. Puljic, Reverend Puljic, clearly called on the Croatian people to stay in their homes and instructed the clergy to assist their people to remain; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, in spite of that, the HVO leadership, or of the HDZ - I can't go into that now, but you may know this - took steps for the HVO to move out of the centre of town and to take up positions at Hajdarove Njive, Bukovica, Mjenica [phoen], heights from which the town could be controlled; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
