utterances.text: I do know that they withdrew, but I do not wish nor can I judge what they wanted to achieve and whether they wanted to do so intentionally. I don't wish to talk about those things. Those are military things that don't concern me, political and military.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, you certainly knew that they withdrew to Dolac, south-east of Travnik, Radica Brdo to west of Travnik, Kalibunar and other locations that I have mentioned. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also certainly know that the HVO, upon leaving Travnik and going towards Guca Gora and Vitez, and in Guca Gora itself, set up checkpoints through which it was impossible to pass without permission of the HVO, and it was not possible to go from Travnik to Zenica. Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also know that from those checkpoints, both soldiers and civilians were turned back, sometimes even sick people who needed to go from the Travnik hospital to the hospital in Zenica?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Now, how you qualify those checkpoints, I don't know, nor can I judge about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: It was heard in town, and you probably are aware of the fact, that on the 1st of June, 1993, the commander, Mehmed Alagic, and his escort were stopped at the checkpoint and disarmed.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I don't know that, but very hazily, but I really didn't make an effort to register these things, nor did I give these things any thought. If there was an incident, I would hear about it, and that's all. It seems to me that far back in my mind, something to that effect was rumoured.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Regarding events and relations in Travnik, you were aware of the fact that open armed conflicts were going on in the Lasva Valley between the army and the HVO, and this certainly affected the situation and the relations in Travnik itself, and this contributed to the heightening of tensions. What I mean is that you all knew that in the spring of 1993, in the Lasva Valley and around Novi Travnik, there was heavy fighting between the army and the HVO. Were you aware of those facts, and did they have a negative impact on relations among people in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I have to say that what was going on outside Travnik, I knew little about those things. I knew that there were some unfortunate conflicts, but I didn't make any judgement of what the policies were or who was the aggressor, who was attacking who, who was provoking who. I simply didn't speculate about those things. I had so much to do in town itself that I kept wondering what would happen to it, as all the military forces of the Croatian people had left and that the civilians were in great fear and that many were leaving the town and coming back again. They would spend a day there and leave overnight, or something like that. And also those who could, left the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Precisely because of the position you held and the job you did, I would never ask you to pass judgement on events. I'm just asking you whether you were familiar with these facts and whether you knew that they had a negative impact on the mood of people in town itself.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I did know that they impacted the atmosphere in town. I knew that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also as a priest, you knew that in the spring of 1993, in April 1993 -- let me not qualify it, but an HVO attacked Ahmici entailing many victims and the destruction of many religious buildings of the Islamic faith, which also could have had negative consequences regarding the town of Travnik itself. Were you aware of those facts?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I claim with full responsibility that I did not. I was so preoccupied with other activities. I heard of something subsequently, but at the time, and regarding the intensity of the events, I was not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, it is quite possible, and I'm asking you whether you knew that the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, through practical acts and through orders, endeavoured to prevent any kind of retaliation and to protect Catholic religious buildings and Catholic priests issuing prior orders and especially orders following armed conflicts. Are you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I know nothing about any such order. After the conflict, no piece of paper could help me. I was just wondering what would happen to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, for identification purposes, I would like to show the witness two orders issued by the 3rd Corps, and this will lead to some additional questions of mine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could a copy of these two orders be shown to the witness, and both documents were received by the Defence from the Prosecutor within the framework of the Sarajevo collection of documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I didn't interrupt all the time. Also, the witness always said basically: "I don't know." But this time, he was asked by my learned friend about orders, and the witness said: "I know nothing about any such order. After the conflict, no piece of paper could help me." I really have my doubts as to whether Defence should be allowed to show the witness orders after he very, very clearly stated that he just doesn't know about such orders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Go ahead and ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I've shown this document for the witness to identify, and I just want to refresh the witness's memory.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Could you have a look at this order dated the 10th of June, issued after the armed conflict in Travnik. And have a look at item 3.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Do I have to comment on this?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to ask you whether you are aware of the fact that the army took steps to protect buildings, and you personally, as a religious official.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I believe that that is the case, but I have never seen this document before. I've never had the opportunity of reading it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, the witness has answered my question. He has told us what he was aware of, and I didn't think that I could tender this document into evidence through this witness. But given the relevance of the document and the fact that the witness doesn't contest the document and the further questions will have to do with the actual situation the witness was in, for these reasons, I suggest that these documents be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, in this instance, the Prosecution objects to even mark the document for identification. The witness said: "I have never seen this order." He just doesn't know. If this is allowed to continue, each party, in future, may show any document to a witness. The witness says: "I've never seen the document. I don't know about," but we mark it for identification. This procedure appears to be highly problematic, and the Prosecution objects against marking this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The second document, we'll decide about this in a minute, after the break. Ask the question concerning the second document.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkic, have you had a look at the second document, dated the 19th?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'm looking at it now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: This document clearly shows that after the events that had happened, the command repeated its previous orders about protecting private and public buildings and property. The document contains a date, subsequently to the time when you left Travnik. But my question is: Are you aware of the fact that members of the army attempted to protect property and prevent damage from being done? In fact, they asked for all those involved in such acts to be punished. It was forbidden to commit such acts. Are you aware of such steps having been taken?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President --

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Was this part of your experience while you were in Travnik?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, two objections. If Your Honours please have a look at the question. The question starts with a comment. This is certainly not a question to the witness. This appears to be highly problematic. My learned friend from the Defence herself is making reference to the fact that this document refers to a time after the witness had left Travnik. It's very difficult to understand the purpose and how the witness can -- the purpose of showing this document to the witness, the relevance, and how the witness may be able to comment on the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I only showed the witness the document to remind the witness of what he personally knew about how the army behaved, and my question was clear. My question was: Were you a witness of the fact that members of the army took steps to protect property, and they attempted to punish the perpetrators of such acts?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I was not in a position to be an eyewitness of such events. I couldn't perform my duties as a priest. I wasn't free to move around after everything had escalated. All I could observe was that shops were broken into and nothing was done. I could also see the Mujahedin driving away in cars. They would seize cars by force. They had weapons, not just rifles, which they would mount on cars. They would demonstrate, they would parade around with flags. I believe that the army took such steps, in official terms, but in practical terms, on the basis of what I could see in the city I moved around in -- well, I didn't have the experience that you have described. Because in the centre of the town, they would break into places, destroy facilities, and if a car is stolen, then property isn't protected. And if we are threatened, if people break into houses without warrants of any kind, then the situation is very insecure. And I would also like to point out that I was given a piece of paper, a small piece of paper, about this size, and perhaps it was Hadzihasanovic who wrote these things down. I couldn't say exactly who did this, because I was in a very difficult situation. But the note said that Mr. Mirko Ivkic is protected by Bosnia and Herzegovina. I won't cover this up, but given my experiences, I would claim that the contrary was in fact the case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, having heard this explanation, given that these documents are important and will be referred to by the Defence in the course of the proceedings, and as they relate to command responsibility, I also suggest that these documents be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is the first time I've seen these documents.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution again objects marking this document for identification. The witness has said: "I've never seen the document." Answering the question of my learned friend, the witness has said: It's to the contrary. Again, the Prosecution considers this manner to mark documents for identification as being very problematic, since it would result in a situation that any party can show any document to a witness, the witness may say whatever he or she wants, and the document is then marked for identification. That appears to be extremely problematic, and the Prosecution, for that reason, objects against marking this document for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will have our break now and we will resume at five to 1.00 and inform you of our decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will resume now. As far as the request to tender the documents into evidence is concerned, documents of the -- dated the 19th of June, 1993, and another document dated the 19th of June, 1993, which had to do with Article 3, concerns the protection of religious buildings. The Trial Chamber has decided to mark these documents for identification. The Trial Chamber would like to point out to both parties that when we decide to mark a document for identification, this means that the document is on standby. It isn't a document that has been admitted into evidence at this stage. It can only be admitted into evidence if this document is tendered through another witness, or if the document is supported by other elements. So when we say that a document has been marked for identification, this means that, in legal terms, the document has not been admitted into evidence, but it is marked for identification just to keep track of a document which we think might have relevance. For this reason, we mark documents for identification. But when the Trial Chamber says that a document has been marked for identification, this isn't tantamount to admitting it into evidence. I want this to be absolutely clear. A document marked for identification has not yet been admitted into evidence. We will decide about the fate of the document in question at a later date. A document admitted into evidence has to be supported, confirmed by other witness or by other information, by other elements. Having said that, Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for this document which will be marked for identification. Could we have a standby number for this document.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the order dated 10th of June, 1993 gets the Exhibit number DH64, marked for identification. Its English translation gets the Exhibit number DH64/E, marked for identification. Then the order dated 19th of June, 1993 gets the Exhibit number DH65, marked for identification; and its English translation gets the Exhibit number DH65/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] For the moment, we have some documents that have been marked for identification. Once the Prosecution has concluded its case, or once the Defence has concluded its case, we'll decide about the fate of the other documents on standby. We'll have a special hearing to discuss this matter, and if other elements don't support these documents, these documents will be rejected. So when we say that a document has been marked for identification - and I want this to be absolutely clear - it only means that we are giving the document a number, but this document has not been admitted into evidence. Documents admitted into evidence will be given a definitive exhibit number. So in each such occasion, as you have observed, I ask the registrar to provide us with a definitive exhibit number. If a document is marked for identification, it hadn't yet been admitted into evidence. I hope that the Prosecution has understood what I have said, in order to make sure that there is nothing ambiguous. The Defence may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkic, I hope that you have had the chance to rest. Can we continue now? In the course of the examination-in-chief, you said that the escalation of the conflict started at the beginning of June, and I would like to ask you whether it would be correct to say that the conflict lasted for a number of days and finished at the end of the first week in June in 1993. Is that correct? The armed conflict.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The armed conflict did not come to an end in the first week.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that, together with HVO units which were withdrawing from Travnik, some of the Croatian population from the town of Travnik also withdrew; they withdrew together? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. In fact, they withdrew in accordance with an already adopted plan for evacuation and the request that they should leave the area in which there was a conflict with the army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: And you, as a man and a priest, objected to this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I wouldn't want to give you the wrong answer to the question. It's not quite clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I will ask you two questions. First of all, as a priest and as a Bosnian --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. As I said, you should proceed question by question. Otherwise, the witness might become confused. So split the question up into two questions, and this will enable everyone to find their bearings. Otherwise, if the witness says yes or no, we're not sure which part of the question the witness is answering.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I will rephrase the question and divide it into two parts to make things absolutely clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Would it be correct to say that you, as a Bosniak, as a Croatian Bosnian and as a priest, objected to people leaving their homes and their town? You did not agree with this; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, under the influence of propaganda and you already -- and the plan that had been agreed on to evacuate the town, the people withdrew with the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I don't believe I can say that this was the influence of propaganda. I know that when I made a statement on the radio, this is what I had to say and it's not something that I believed in. Because when the people flee, then they're fleeing from their homes. It can't be the result of propaganda. Arms must be used if people are fleeing.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of the fact that some of the population fled from the town, from the area that was under the control of the Serbian forces?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Were you aware of the fact that at the time, the HVO was already cooperating with the Serbian forces in situations when there was a conflict with the BH army?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: No, I wasn't aware of that. I later heard that there was no other possible solution. They had to establish peace with the other side, with the former common enemy, so to speak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, according to your testimony before this Court, you personally remained in the parish office with the priest Vinko Vidakovic, and the cook Finka Rajic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. I did remain there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Also, as you testified earlier on, you were active in the Caritas office in distributing aid to refugees, not just Croats, but also Bosniaks; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to you in the Caritas office, there was Ivan Petric, Zvonko Kukric, Dzevko Gaca [phoen], and Franjo Mikic; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the armed conflict, there was a high degree of chaos in town; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: During the first days of the armed conflict, a soldier came to your office who asked you to get in touch with Commander Leutar, who was at Radica Brdo because his family was there and he asked you to try and intervene on his behalf for the family to be protected; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: That was on the second day, if I'm not mistaken. That is at the very beginning, when there was the fiercest clash between the armed forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: As a man and as a priest you thought you should try and help this soldier?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that at the time of these conflicts, several soldiers entered the parish office to search it and to check whether there were any weapons in the office; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is. When they came to ask, not really to ask, but this was conditioned. Our aid to them was conditioned by adequate treatment of us. That is when they searched the premises.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: They didn't find the weapons, but they didn't take anything from the parish office or the church?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: They didn't enter the church on that occasion. However, they didn't take anything from the parish building except I think there was a pair of binoculars, a civilian pair of binoculars of my priest in his room, and if I recollect well, it was taken away.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When, in such a chaotic situation, a group of soldiers entered Caritas and they wanted to seize a part of the foodstuffs that were stored there, they listed those supplies and you signed it as being a donation, because in the circumstances, you felt that it would be the best thing to do rather than to resist; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In that period of time, both the civilian and military authorities, through the public media, called on Croats to stay in their homes and to return to their homes. Did you hear those calls?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: In addition to such calls, if I registered them correctly, there were actually announcements calling on the Croats to report and to come to a collection point, those of them who were still in town, and to be engaged for some purposes. I assume that this was manipulation, because I once was given one information, and another time, another. They were intended to be organised for some sort of labour. There were rumours of large numbers of dead. And I refused that. They asked me to call on the people to come out of their houses and to be engaged for work.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true, Mr. Ivkic, that in those first days, or the first week of the month of June, you did contact representatives of the civilian authorities in Travnik and that one of them told you on that occasion that it would be a good idea for you to make a speech on the media?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: As my house was under a blockade and the general blockade outside, I couldn't act at all. When the situation calmed down a little and when they contacted me, I heard of the drama going on behind Ovcarevo, in the area toward the Serbs, that a large number of people had gathered there and that they were about to move towards Serb positions, where they would be taken in by the Serbs. And this disturbed me, and I wanted to go there and get in touch with those people.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: We'll come to that later. But I'm now asking you the following: When things calmed down a little in Travnik, did you communicate with representatives of the civilian authorities in Travnik, and did they, for the purpose of calming the situation and encouraging people to return home, that it would be a good idea for you to make an announcement on the public media? Was this suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: First it was I who suggested that an intervention be made and for me to be allowed to go there, and only after the exodus occurred, I suggested that I should speak on the radio, but only after this had happened did they offer me to make this broadcast, to make a public statement.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: But as a man and as a priest who had throughout insisted on people staying in their homes, you felt it would be useful and a good idea for the Croats of Travnik to be addressed by you, as a priest, when you would suggest to them not to leave their homes; is that true? You sincerely wanted that and you made such an attempt; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that because of the general chaos, there were some verbal provocations, and talking to Mr. Asim Gradincic, a representative of the civilian authorities, you told him that you didn't feel quite safe and that you would like to have some sort of protection; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I didn't just feel it; I experienced it. I -- already there was pressure on the house as a building and on us, as the people living in it. But I also wish to point out that the departure of the Croatian people disturbed me so much that I was absolutely shocked. I was out of my mind. I cried more than ever in my whole life.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, tell me, please: Is it true that you did address Asim Gradincic, a representative of the civilian authorities, and conveyed to him your fears and apprehensions and your request for protection, not just for yourself, but the parish office and the church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true that immediately after that, both the military and the civilian authorities reacted and designated two members of the BH army from the protective platoon to watch over you and the parish office on a permanent basis; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: If I may remind you: Those members of the army were Mulam Imamovic and Indjic Besim.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember either name. I know that one was called Dino and he was a waiter in a coffee bar near the market. I knew him, but not the others. I couldn't even remember what they looked like. But this one person I did know, Dino he was called. And there were two of them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Actually, the presence of two members of the army was provided all the time and who took care of your security round the clock; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: They were present in the house. As for security that I wanted to talk to him about, the soldiers were in the house and they were there. But they didn't mistreat us, nor did they represent a threat to us.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let us now go back to the event that you said happened on the 7th. And if I tell you that the event actually happened on the 8th of June, would you agree with me?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes. When I said the 7th, this was something I was reminded of when this event was discussed, but I'm sure that somewhere the date is registered. So it's quite possible that I may be wrong. Whether it was the 7th or the 8th.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: That morning, about half past 7.00 or 8.00, you were woken up by Mrs. Finka Rajic, who told you that she thought somebody was attacking the church?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: No, not that she thought that someone was attacking it, but that it was happening. She told us of that. But as soon as I opened my eyes, I realised that it was true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: She also told you that in front of the church there was a foreigner, Mujahedin, and that bangings could be heard inside?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, and I saw him immediately as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw this Mujahedin in front of the church, as you already said, you called up the police immediately and the civilian authorities, the people whose telephone numbers you had in the office?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, correct. And in each call, I inquired about any other authorities that I should call up, and I asked those that I was talking to to pass on this information and to take steps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The soldiers who were in the office to take care of your safety came out and headed towards the church, but one of the Mujahedin hit the soldier with his rifle butt, the soldier fell on the ground, and afterwards, they went into the parish office and locked themselves up; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I can't confirm that. I know what the soldier told me. He said that he had been hit and that they had run into the house and locked themselves in. And that is true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When you saw this Mujahedin and called up the civilian and military authorities, you climbed up to the attic of the parish building and you stayed there until Ms. Rajic called you and told you that the soldiers had arrived and chased away the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: That was at the end, when we expected them to break into the house as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Finka Rajic informed you that it was safe, you came down and you saw in front of the church quite a number of people. The Mujahedin were no longer there, they had left, but there were members of the army and some representatives of the civilian authorities; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I wasn't watching from the house. I went downstairs and I saw these people in front of the door, the people who had arrived.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Representatives of the public security station, the MUP of Travnik, also arrived, and they immediately carried out an on-site inspection of what had happened in the church; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I should like the witness to be shown a document of the report on the on-site inspection and the criminal reports in connection with this incident, as the witness has confirmed this. And once it has been shown to the witness, I should like to tender it into evidence. At the same time, I should like to inform Your Honours that during the investigation, the Defence found this document in the archives of the district prosecutor's office in Travnik, where the documents of the district military prosecutor's office in Travnik are also kept.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkic, at the time, you immediately told members of the police of your first impression regarding the damage, and you said that you thought that the damage was of incalculable value. During the investigation, it was quite clear that the raid had been done by eight to ten Mujahedin and that they were not members of the army; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After these answers by the witness, and as it is a relevant document in our submission, I should like to tender it into evidence as a Defence exhibit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What is the position of the Prosecution regarding the tendering of this document? Actually, there are two documents, two translations that we have.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution doesn't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Chamber wishes to note that, contrary to what the Defence has said that the Mujahedin were not members of the army, the document indicates that they were members of the Muslim forces.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. They were not members of the Army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, as the Defence has sought to show on a number of occasions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Registrar, we have two documents, therefore. Could you give us exhibit numbers for each of those documents, together with their English translations.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the document dated -- the document number 198/02 230 150, criminal complaint, gets the exhibit number DH65, marked for -- 66, marked for identification. And its English translation gets Exhibit number DH --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is not to be marked for identification. These are documents that are being finally admitted as exhibits. So these are final numbers.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I apologise. Okay. The Exhibit number will be DH66, and the exhibit number of the English translation gets the Exhibit number DH66/E. And then the document titled "record on investigation" gets the Exhibit number DH67, and the English translation gets the Exhibit number DH67/E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkic, you have already said that with the officials who arrived after your call, Fikret Cuskic also arrived, who -- you said Cuskic, and I suggest it was Fikret Cuskic, commander of the 17th Krajina Brigade; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Gradincic also arrived, who was the one who communicated with you most frequently on behalf of the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: He was the contact person throughout that period.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: The Travnik mufti also arrived, with whom you had good, friendly relations up until then; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I don't remember that the mufti arrived. There wasn't a single religious official coming to see me. I don't remember that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Commander Cuskic expressed his regret on account of what had happened and said that the Mujahedin should be killed; is that right?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: By saying that, he let me know that he did not agree with what had been done.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Immediately after the inspection, and after the officials had toured the church, members of the civil defence came and assisted in cleaning the church after the mess that had been made by the Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The church was cleaned shortly after that. Regarding the cleaning of the church, Finka Rajic should be asked, because she did her best to do it, and I think that the civil defence people did assist up to a point. They did show readiness to do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mrs. Rajic managed to put away the damaged sculptures so that, as you testified today, some of them could be repaired, as you have testified today?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: The objects were broken, and as such, they were put to one side in the church or in the sacristy. The possibility of repairing them was something that I was unable to judge at that point in time, but the scope of destruction was very considerable.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: For the sake of the transcript, could Mrs. Rajic's name be noted as Finka, "F", and not Finka, as noted on page 75, line 14. Finka, F-i-n-k-a.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Ivkic, a moment ago you said that you asked for permission to go to a place where the refugee population was located when answering questions put to you previously you said that from an army commander you received permission, in fact, a document which showed that you were under the protection of the army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: It was a piece of paper. It wasn't even A4 format. It was a piece of paper, and I remember the exact words. It said that I was under the protection of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In addition to that piece of paper, you were provided with two other permits, although one mistakenly stated that your name was Ukic [as interpreted] instead of Ivkic, and your name was mistakenly represented. Instead of Mirko, it was Ivko. In order to remind you about this, I would like to show the witness two -- the two documents to the witness that have to do with his -- with permission given to him to move around the area.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: To move around the area of Ovcarevo and Plakarevo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the Defence tell us where these documents come from, the documents that they are presenting now.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence found these documents in the course of its investigations in the archives in Travnik. That's where they were found.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. I have to tell you that I'm not familiar with these documents. I've never had them before me. And I wouldn't have said that my name was Fabo or Ivo. I would have said that my name was Mirko. That's a significant difference. And likewise, Babic, Dr. Zdravko Babic, I can't remember anyone who that is name. Kemal Sisic, a driver, perhaps. This is an internal document. I've never seen these documents before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, since the witness can't identify these documents, I won't be suggesting that they be marked for identification, but I have a question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, would it be correct to say that you were given permission to go to Ovcarevo, and you in fact did go there?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it's correct. I did go to Ovcarevo, to the place called Ovcarevo, which is a village. I was taken there and returned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: However, unfortunately, as you said a while ago, it was late, because the population that had waited there for a few days had already crossed the lines and left the area of Travnik municipality; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In response to a question put to you by the Prosecution -- yes, please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I'd like to say that this is not correct. When it mentions a Yugo vehicle, the vehicle concerned was not a Yugo vehicle.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Since you can't identify the documents and the documents refer to you, I've withdrawn my suggestion to have these documents admitted into evidence, and you have told me, in your own words, how you went to Ovcarevo. I'm quite content with your answer. Thank you. In response to a question put to you by my learned colleague from the Prosecution, you also said that you wanted to establish contact, communications with the bishop in Sarajevo and the BH army made this possible for you. You were able to do so from their communications centre; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: From Mr. Puljic -- you asked Mr. Puljic to come to Travnik, if he could, in order to visit the church and to make sure that the church could continue to function as usual; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You also explained that he was not able to come immediately because the bishopric in Sarajevo had been shelled by the Serbian forces. But he took advantage of the first opportunity to come and visit, and in the second half of June, he came to Travnik; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He came in UNPROFOR vehicles?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, because of the fierce fighting in the surroundings of Travnik, from another -- it wasn't possible to come to Travnik from other parts of Bosnia and Herzegovina unless UNPROFOR provided assistance; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: So this was a result of the situation. The fact that the HVO and the army were fighting each other. At that time, they could not communicate; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes. They were involved in a conflict. That's correct. But they also had the possibility of communicating through UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally weren't able to address UNPROFOR, to contact UNPROFOR and to inform them of your desire to leave Travnik. You couldn't do this before Mr. Puljic arrived?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: That's correct, and that's what was most terrible. I wasn't able to contact anyone else. I wasn't able to contact the journalists or UNPROFOR. I could only contact Asim Gradincic. It was through Asim Gradincic that I could contact the town authorities, but not in relation to everything that I wanted to contact them about. This was done -- contact was established when they wished contact to be established. I'd like to say that sometimes I was forced to do this. Arms were used to force me to do this.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: When Mr. Puljic, the Bosnian bishop, arrived in Travnik, he was received as a prominent guest and he was given all the honours that such guests are given; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You took advantage of the situation -- I'll ask you a different question. When Bishop Puljic arrived on the 19th of June, that's when he arrived in Travnik, at that time the church was already functioning. Masses could be celebrated in the church. It had been cleaned up and the objects that had been damaged had been removed and it was possible to use the church; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: No, it's not correct. It's true that the church had been cleaned up, but it wasn't functioning properly, and I was not in a position to perform my duties in the church at the time. I was involved in other matters at the time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You personally, as a man, were affected by the entire situation and by the fact that you couldn't retain the local inhabitants in the town. You were personally afraid, and as you said, you took advantage of the situation and you got into an UNPROFOR vehicle and left Travnik in this manner; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: You were replaced by the priest Pavo Nikolic; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: He immediately started performing his duties, because at the time, St. John the Baptist's feast was approaching and the BH army made it possible for this day to be celebrated as best as possible; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I heard. I know that that's what happened. But that does not mean that Pavo had the same experience as I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the witness has said that he has heard about this, that he is aware of the fact that this happened, I'll show the witness a document from the BH army. This document shows that the army took steps to ensure that this important saint's day be celebrated. So I would like this witness to be shown the document, and I'd now like to suggest that the document be marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: I'd just like to repeat the question once more. You know that the BH army and the local authorities took steps to ensure that, on the 24th of June, 1993, the saint's day be celebrated in the church of St. John the Baptist. You're aware of this fact, are you not?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Yes, I'm aware of this fact. It's irrelevant for me.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ivkic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could this document be marked for identification. And I have no further questions for the witness. This document was found in the Travnik archives in the course of the Defence's investigations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before we mark the document for identification, I would like to know what the Prosecution's position is. And I would also like to point out the following: It seems that the Defence is claiming that the army took steps for protection. When we have a look at the document, at the beginning of the letter, we can see that it is in fact a response to a request which was apparently compiled by the priest, Nikolic. So it's a response to a request. It's not a personal initiative taken by Mr. Alagic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. We have shown other documents in which it mentions the attempts of the civilian protection. It mentions on-site investigations, et cetera. Naturally, the new priest addressed these people with regard to the saint's day. And as you can see from the letter, the army accepted to help the church celebrate this day.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I have --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What I wanted to say was not quite that. Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, I wish to express my concerns if my learned friend tries to testify before this Court in respect to the marking for identification of this document, in light of the -- today's decision of the Trial Chamber and in light of the additional explanations given to the decision, the Prosecution doesn't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We will mark the document for identification, which means that this document isn't being admitted into evidence, but at some subsequent time, the Defence might provide additional information to support the document. Mr. Registrar, could we have a number for identification.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, the Exhibit number will be DH68, marked for identification, and the English translation gets the Exhibit number DH68/E, marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Thank you. If I have understood you correctly, the Defence has no further questions; is that correct, Ms. Residovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, that's correct. Thank you, Mr. President. Thank you, Mr. Ivkic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Before we adjourn, because we will be adjourning soon, the Trial Chamber has a minor question for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When your church was damaged by these eight or ten individuals, and you said that these individuals were Mujahedin, were these individuals, if you saw them, wearing uniforms? Did you see them personally?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: Not all of them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How many of them did you see?

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: I saw a soldier in front. His uniform was a Mujahedin uniform. It wasn't a traditional, classical uniform such as the ones that BH army soldiers wore. I also saw --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Could you describe the uniform that you saw, for the benefit of the Trial Chamber.

utterances.speaker: MIRKO IVKIC
utterances.text: To tell you the truth, I don't have a clear picture of the uniform. I was afraid at the time, but I noticed that the soldier wasn't wearing a cap. And this upper part, it wasn't really a regular part of a military uniform. It wasn't very neat and proper. He had a rifle. I know for sure that it was a Mujahedin. That's how he looked. That's how he was addressed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. That's what we wanted to know. Mr. Withopf, we have a few more minutes. Do you have any further questions? I didn't think there were any questions for the other Defence team. Mr. Dixon, I'm certain of your response, although I skipped you.

utterances.speaker: MR. DIXON
utterances.text: We have no questions for this witness. As we anticipated, he hasn't testified about any charges against Mr. Kubura. I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Dixon. Yes, Mr. Withopf.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, the Prosecution has no questions in re-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Witness, thank you for having come to The Hague. You have testified in the conditions we decided on at the beginning of the hearing. You have answered the questions put to you both by the Defence and by the Prosecution, and you have also provided the Trial Chamber with certain clarifications. I wish you a good trip back to the country where you act as a priest at the moment. And I will now ask the usher to escort you out of the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. I wish you a lot of success in your work.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll now turn to Mr. Withopf. We are a little late because two witnesses were scheduled for today and we have only heard one of them. Tomorrow we were to have two witnesses. Do you think that both witnesses will be able to -- will be able to be examined tomorrow? What is your assessment of the situation for tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, both witnesses will be made available, obviously. It's hard to anticipate at this stage whether it will be possible to finish with both witnesses tomorrow. However, it could be possible. It depends again, of course, on the length of cross-examination. From what we can anticipate, it could -- or there is some --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And in relation to how long the examination will last.

utterances.speaker: MR. WITHOPF
utterances.text: This is what I was just about to say. I was just about to indicate how long the Prosecution will probably need for the examination-in-chief. Based on our assessment of the examination-in-chief, it may be possible that both witnesses can be concluded tomorrow, but there's obviously no guarantee.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I suggest that in relation to these two witnesses, you should see if one of them might be able to stay on over the weekend, appear for a hearing on Monday. So you should see whether one of the witnesses perhaps has a reason to return home earlier. You could perhaps take steps in order to make sure that the first witness to testify is the one who might have a problem if he had to stay on in The Hague. I think it would be good to pay attention to this issue to ensure that the witnesses testify in the best possible conditions. I apologise to the interpreters for having exceeded the time. We will resume tomorrow at 9.00. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Friday, the 19th day of March, 2004, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.59 p.m.,
